title: Doers of the word (James 1:19–27)
hook: swift to hear, slow to speak, and not hearers only

segments.voice: Yesterday, every best gift, coming down from the Father of lights. Your line was from above. What small good thing did you trace back up? Day six hundred five.

On your way out the door you catch yourself in the hall mirror. Hair sticking up. Something green in your teeth. You see it clearly. You even make a face at it. Then your keys are in your hand, the door shuts behind you, and by the time you reach the car the mirror is gone from your mind, and so is the spinach. Two hours later someone at work tells you. James uses a moment like it, a man and a mirror, to describe the way people listen to God's word.
screen: `THE HALL MIRROR ON THE WAY OUT.` → `YOU SAW IT, THEN FORGOT.` → `JAMES HAS A MIRROR TOO.`

segments.voice: It starts with three speeds. The Douay-Rheims: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger." Fast ears, slow mouth, slower temper. A quarrel runs the other way round. Then the line this whole passage turns on: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." Deceiving yourselves. Hearing can feel like progress. A good homily, a moving reading, a podcast that lands, and it's easy to think, there, that's done. James says that feeling can fool you. And here comes the mirror. Someone who hears the word and doesn't do it, he says, is like a man who looks at his own face in a glass, walks away, and forgets at once what he looked like. The word works like a mirror. It shows you yourself. The question is whether you do anything about what you saw. The Greek for doers is poietai, makers. Greek used the same word for a poet. So a doer of the word is someone who makes something out of what they heard. Then James gets practical. Rein in your tongue. And he gives a short definition of religion that is hard to wriggle out of: religion that's pure in God's sight is this, "to visit the fatherless and widows in their tribulation," and to keep yourself unstained by the world. Not more listening. Visiting. Catholics hear the word at every Mass, and at the end of it the people are sent out: go. The hearing happens inside. The doing happens on the way home.
screen: `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · `HEARING CAN FOOL YOU.` · `THE MAN AT THE MIRROR FORGETS.` · `VISIT THE FATHERLESS AND WIDOWS.` · then, large: `BE YE DOERS OF THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing you heard at Mass. Sit comfortably and breathe. Think back to the last Mass you went to, or, if that was a while ago, to any line of scripture you've heard this week. Let one phrase come back. Don't search for the best one; take the first that sticks. Then ask what it would look like on a Tuesday. A call to make. A visit. An apology. A meal for someone. Picture yourself doing it, today, specifically: where, when, the first words you'd say. If you pray, you can ask for the help to do it. If you don't, just choose it and hold it. The bell holds the time.
Poietai, makers. James one: not hearers only, who see themselves in the mirror and forget, but makers, who do what they heard. Today's word.
Your line: doers, not hearers. Today, do the thing you chose before you go to bed, even in its smallest form. Day six hundred five.

howItsDone: At every Mass Catholics hear readings from scripture and a homily, and the Mass ends with a dismissal sending the people out; many parishes link the Sunday word to works of mercy such as visiting the sick, the elderly and the bereaved.

fork.setup: you've just heard a reading that hit home. you feel moved, and part of you feels the job is done. what does James say?
options: good: being moved is the point.
do something with it, or you're fooling yourself.
talk about it with everyone right away.
fork.reveal: James says hearers only deceive themselves. and talking right away isn't it either: he wants people swift to hear and slow to speak.

original.note: Greek: doers of the word (James 1:22). a poiētēs is a maker; Greek also used the word for a poet.

trapdoor: what you thought: listen in church, then live your life.
what it means: hearing that doesn't turn into doing is like seeing your face in a mirror and forgetting it at once.
what a scholar hears: poietai logou, makers of the word: the hearer is meant to make something of what he heard.

sources.quoted: let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger.

notes: James 1:23–24 (the man beholding his face in a glass) is paraphrased.
Poietes (maker, doer) as the source of English 'poet' (via Latin poeta): standard etymology. Confirm.
'Nineteen centuries before hall mirrors were cheap': mirrors in James's day were polished metal; the line is a light touch. Confirm it reads well.
The dismissal at the end of Mass ('go') is described, not quoted, since the current English texts are not public domain.
